talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Tell the tuner what you want to change and in which direction, rather than dropping the suspension off and hoping. Describe what the bike is doing, not only the setting you think you need.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: A tuner without a direction defaults to a generic setup; symptom descriptions let them pick the circuit.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Say where on the track it happens: braking zone, corner entry / mid / exit, braking bumps, acceleration chop, jump face, landing, whoops, rollers, square edges.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: The same word (e.g. harsh) maps to different circuits depending on terrain and phase of the corner.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Split every complaint into on-throttle (weight rearward, rear squats, front light) or off-throttle (weight forward, fork loaded, rear light).
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Keefer presents this as a shortcut that narrows the problem to fork, shock or chassis and gives rider and tuner a common language.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Say which end and where you feel it in your body: through the hands/bars, the feet/pegs, or the seat; and whether it is rear traction, front traction, or a bump feel.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Hands point to the fork, seat and pegs often to the shock; traction loss vs harshness are different problems.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: For an impact, say whether the bike hit and bounced off (deflected) or hit and sank into the stroke.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Deflecting usually means too stiff or too slow; sinking means too soft. Bones Bacon's example of a question tuners must ask.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Say whether the problem is on the first bump or builds over a series of bumps (gets lower and lower, gets harsher after several hits).
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Good on the first bump but harsh after several, or the rear getting progressively lower, points to rebound too slow (packing) rather than compression.
talking_to_your_tuner.quote: the rear of the bike just keeps getting lower and lower

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: When you say harsh, say whether it feels stiff (not using travel) or soft (sitting low in the stroke and hitting the ramp-up).
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Harshness can come from either direction and the fixes are opposite.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Avoid asking for 'plush'; say 'bump absorption' or describe the specific bump you want handled better.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Keefer warns techs may read 'plush' as a request for a very soft setup.
talking_to_your_tuner.quote: be careful when using this term with suspension techs as they may want to set your suspension up too soft.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Vague statements like 'I get headshake' or 'it kicks' are not enough; specify lock-to-lock bar swapping vs a light jittery front, and whether a kick is compression, rebound or spring related as far as you can tell (or describe when it happens).
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Tuners say most riders cannot say what the suspension is doing, so they must keep questioning or watch the rider.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Be honest about weight, speed and skill level; do not overstate ability.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Overstating ability gets a setup that is too stiff; Factory Connection and MXA both stress honesty.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: If a change made no noticeable difference, say so instead of telling the tuner what you think they want to hear.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Invented differences send tuning in the wrong direction; testers are told the same.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Tell the tuner whether you want a performance setup (firm support, resists blow-through, for fast/heavy riders) or a comfort setup (more stroke use, smoother small bumps, may bottom on big hits).
talking_to_your_tuner.why: This is the main trade-off a valving choice makes.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Before blaming valving, report or check rider sag, spring rate for your weight, fork height in clamps, tire pressure, steering head bearing, fork torque/binding and linkage lube.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: These produce symptoms that look like damping problems; e.g. loose head bearing causes headshake, bound forks feel harsh after a revalve.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Keep detailed notes of what feels good and bad and send them, so the tuner is not guessing.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Notes give the tuner a record of conditions and changes.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: After a revalve, if it feels wrong, return to base settings, change one circuit at a time a couple of clicks, then contact the tuner with specific feedback; shops offer updated settings or guarantees.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Changing compression and rebound together hides which one helped; Race Tech publicly invited email feedback for updated settings.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Know what was actually done: a service (oil, seals) or a respring will not feel like a revalve; a revalve also will not fix everything, and many riders expect perfection immediately.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Mismatched expectations are a common source of 'no difference' complaints.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Be open to your first diagnosis being backwards; even a pro tester thought a shock was too firm initially and found it was too soft once he stiffened low-speed.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Rider perception of direction is unreliable, which is why tuners use small test changes.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: A tuner may watch you ride to confirm what you describe; if they cannot see it, they narrow it down by location and specific feel before changing anything.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Observation plus targeted questions is how Bones Bacon describes a tuner's process.

talking_to_your_tuner.advice: Mention behaviour at both ends even if the complaint is about one; a change at one end affects the other.
talking_to_your_tuner.why: Keefer frames every adjustment as action and reaction across the machine.
talking_to_your_tuner.quote: The action of one change can have reaction on the opposite end of the machine as well, not just the focused area.

glossary.riders_mean: The suspension stays compressed over a series of bumps and the bike rides lower and lower; rear won't hook up in chop, or front feels light, skips, or shakes mid-corner.
glossary.usually_points_to: Rebound too slow for the bump frequency, sometimes compression too soft letting the wheel dive deep.
glossary.ambiguity: Distinguish from too-soft compression, which shows up immediately (instant dive or bottoming) rather than building up. Teknik also uses packing for a side kick in loam.

glossary.riders_mean: A jarring, firm hit through bars, pegs or seat.
glossary.usually_points_to: Either too stiff (not using travel) or too soft (riding low in the stroke where valving ramps up); also slow rebound, wrong sag, overspring, fork binding/torque.
glossary.ambiguity: The most ambiguous term: fixes are opposite depending on cause. Keefer says a slightly stiffer setting can feel plusher when the bike is riding too low.

glossary.riders_mean: Soft, supple bump absorption at speed; also used for frame feel.
glossary.usually_points_to: Softer compression or faster rebound.
glossary.ambiguity: Tuners may take it as a request for a very soft setup; Keefer prefers 'bump absorption'.

glossary.riders_mean: Little or no resistance; suspension seems to fall through its stroke, especially at the end.
glossary.usually_points_to: More damping (low-speed or rebound depending on where it is felt); spring too light may also bottom.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer 2020 says simply 'more damping'; 2024 specifies low-speed or rebound by location. 'Empty' is also an engine term in Keefer's glossary. 'Dead' was not defined by any source read.

glossary.riders_mean: Suspension dives through the travel on a hard hit with little resistance.
glossary.usually_points_to: Stiffer compression via clickers or valving, usually low-speed; extra fork oil helps but costs early-stroke comfort.
glossary.ambiguity: Overlaps with 'empty' and 'no hold-up'.

glossary.riders_mean: Wanting the fork or shock to sit higher and not sink/blow through, e.g. on decel bumps, jump faces, g-outs.
glossary.usually_points_to: More compression damping (shock HSC adds hold-up in g-outs and jump faces), or heavier spring / more oil.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer's own fix list varies by year (stiffer compression in 2020/2021; oil, spring or damping in 2024).

glossary.riders_mean: Hitting the end of travel hard on landings or big hits.
glossary.usually_points_to: Too soft compression, too little preload/spring, or rebound too slow (packing into bottom). Keefer: bottoming more than 2-3 times per lap means too soft.
glossary.ambiguity: Some bottoming per lap is considered normal; a harsh bottoming jolt is sometimes just called 'harsh'.

glossary.riders_mean: Bike bounces off a bump or square edge instead of absorbing it, pinballs, loses line; rider may roll off.
glossary.usually_points_to: Too stiff (often initial compression), slow rebound, overspring, too-rigid chassis; on-throttle fork deflection can come from rear sag setting.
glossary.ambiguity: Bones Bacon uses deflect-vs-sink as the key question; riders may also call it 'kick' or 'harsh'.

glossary.riders_mean: Rear end thrown up or sideways, often over braking bumps or under power.
glossary.usually_points_to: Shock too soft in compression on braking bumps (Keefer); rebound too fast; or packing (soften rebound) vs bottoming (add compression) per Teknik; fork air too low can cause rear kick (Keefer fork).
glossary.ambiguity: Forum tuner lumpy790 says riders say 'kicking' without knowing if it is compression, rebound or spring. Keefer's on/off-throttle article does not use the word at all.

glossary.riders_mean: Not defined by any source read; used informally for the rear throwing the rider forward off a jump face.
glossary.usually_points_to: Not established from sources this pass.
glossary.ambiguity: Unverified; overlaps with kick and with the seat-bounce technique debate.

glossary.riders_mean: Bike rocks front to rear on and off throttle: front dives when rolling off, rear squats on gas.
glossary.usually_points_to: Soft fork, heavy engine braking, soft shock HSC, too little sag; fixes heavier spring or more low-speed damping.
glossary.ambiguity: Same word for front dive and rear squat; riders may only describe one half.

glossary.riders_mean: Rear sinks under acceleration out of corners.
glossary.usually_points_to: Soft shock compression (HSC/LSC) or too much sag; part of 'pitching' in Keefer's usage.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer folds it into pitching; the word 'squat' itself barely appears in his shock article.

glossary.riders_mean: Front drops too much under braking or off throttle.
glossary.usually_points_to: Soft fork compression, fast rebound, or fork too high in clamps; high rear sag or stiff shock can push front down.
glossary.ambiguity: Overlaps with pitching and with tuck.

glossary.riders_mean: Bike floats/rolls through rollers and waves, vague and under-supported.
glossary.usually_points_to: Soft shock low-speed compression or soft HSC; too-soft chassis rigidity.
glossary.ambiguity: Also used for chassis flex and for air springs with too much volume.

glossary.riders_mean: Bike's attitude feels unbalanced front-to-rear while seated; conventionally rear high and front low.
glossary.usually_points_to: Rear ride height / sag setting.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer 2025 describes it as a rear-high feel while seated; Keefer 2021 lists it under sag that is 'too high', which reads as too much sag (rear low). 'Sag too high/low' is itself ambiguous between the sag number and the rear's ride height. Ask riders whether the rear feels high or low.

glossary.riders_mean: Bars oscillate side to side, from light jitter to violent lock-to-lock swapping.
glossary.usually_points_to: Loose steering head bearings (check first), fork too stiff or rebound too slow/fast on throttle, rear too low/soft making front light, excessive fork dive under braking.
glossary.ambiguity: Bones distinguishes lock-to-lock swapping from a light jittery front; Keefer fork article ties it to fast rebound, MXA to slow rebound. 'Chopper' not found in sources.

glossary.riders_mean: Rear moves side to side under throttle.
glossary.usually_points_to: Rear ride height too high or too low; fast shock rebound at slight lean.
glossary.ambiguity: Riders also use 'swapping' for front bar headshake.

glossary.riders_mean: Front turns in too sharply or falls in mid-corner.
glossary.usually_points_to: Soft fork compression letting it dive (steepening head angle), forks raised in clamps, soft shock compression off throttle, unequal fork clickers.
glossary.ambiguity: Forum riders use 'tuck' and 'knife' interchangeably.

glossary.riders_mean: Front end folds/drops in at or just after braking before turn-in.
glossary.usually_points_to: Forum suggestions: soft fork diving, too much fork rebound (packing), sharp brake bite, weight distribution.
glossary.ambiguity: Not defined by any tuner or tester read; forum posters disagree on causes and on fork height direction.

glossary.riders_mean: Front tire plows wide mid-corner instead of holding the line.
glossary.usually_points_to: Fork too stiff, forks dropped in clamps, soft shock HSC or too much sag letting rear sit low, fast shock rebound.
glossary.ambiguity: Sometimes conflated with 'wash'.

glossary.riders_mean: Front loses grip and slides out, especially at lean or in sand.
glossary.usually_points_to: Vague front from stiff fork, wrong offset, tire compound/pressure; Teknik: front too low relative to rear in sand.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer calls it 'vague'; overlap with push.

glossary.riders_mean: Unclear front traction at lean.
glossary.usually_points_to: Fork too stiff, wrong clamp offset, tire compound or pressure, too little sag.
glossary.ambiguity: Feel word, not a cause.

glossary.riders_mean: Rear tire drives forward under throttle rather than spinning or hopping.
glossary.usually_points_to: Shock rebound speed, sag, compression on acceleration chop; also engine and gearing.
glossary.ambiguity: Keefer uses 'connectivity' for an engine term; poor hook-up is not always suspension.

glossary.riders_mean: Stiff initial part of an air fork stroke you push through before it gets compliant.
glossary.usually_points_to: Lower air pressure, less low-speed damping, lower oil level.
glossary.ambiguity: Air-fork specific.

glossary.riders_mean: How much tire feels like it is on the ground; confidence to get on the gas.
glossary.usually_points_to: Lower tire pressure, softer settings, offset change.
glossary.ambiguity: Feel term.

glossary.riders_mean: Firm supportive setup vs soft compliant setup.
glossary.usually_points_to: Overall valving and spring direction.
glossary.ambiguity: Describes intent, not a symptom.

glossary.riders_mean: Sharp hit through the bars on fast impacts.
glossary.usually_points_to: Not established from MX sources read (only an MTB glossary, excluded).
glossary.ambiguity: Unverified for MX.

glossary.riders_mean: Bouncy, under-damped feel after bumps.
glossary.usually_points_to: Not established from MX sources read; Teknik maps 'rear bounces up off jumps' and 'hops on braking bumps' to too little/too fast rebound.
glossary.ambiguity: Term itself not found in MX tuner sources.

test_log.item: Starting clicker positions (counted from fully in) before any change
test_log.why: Lets you return to baseline and tell the tuner what was run.
Conditions change through the day (Keefer logged sandy morning vs hardpack afternoon).
Soft ground wants stiffer settings, hardpack softer; air fork pressure moves with heat.

test_log.item: Fork: compression, rebound, spring rate or air pressure, preload, oil level, fork height in clamps
Shock: LSC, HSC, rebound, spring rate, preload, sag, shock length, link

test_log.why: Pressure changes contact patch and mimics suspension changes.

test_log.item: Rider weight, engine hours, bike and mods
test_log.why: Context for comparing logs over time.

test_log.item: Score vs baseline (3 = baseline, 3+ slightly better, 3.5 better in most areas, 4 better everywhere, below 3 unacceptable)
Free-text feel notes: what the bike did, where, and what changed
Every change with date, kept as a notebook
test_log.why: Reverse changes that did not help; schedule service.

test_day_structure.step: Check basics: spring rate for weight, sag, tire pressure, head bearing, fork torque
Establish baseline (stock settings or current settings recorded)
test_day_structure.why: Every test is judged against it.

test_day_structure.step: Pick a consistent section/loop with the features that show the problem; ride the same lines at race pace
test_day_structure.why: Comparable results; a casual-pace setting may not hold up racing.

test_day_structure.step: Change one adjuster at a time, small steps (1-2 clicks; Showa about 1, KYB/WP about 2; rebound 1)
Short sessions: 2-4 laps MX per setting, max 15-20 min loop off-road
test_day_structure.why: Keep the baseline memory fresh and avoid second-guessing.

test_day_structure.step: Back-to-back comparisons, about 3-4 combinations then return to baseline
Test specific features per circuit: small bumps (fork comp), sweepers (fork rebound), worst hit (bottoming), acceleration bumps (shock comp), braking bumps and jumps (shock rebound), whoops (packing)
Score and note after each session
Limit parts/settings per day; pick best two per day, decide on a final day
Stop when comfortable; don't chase every condition change
test_day_structure.why: You can tune yourself to a standstill.

disagreements.positions: Keefer: 1-2 clicks at a time. Vital forum (Pirate421): about 5 clicks so the change is noticeable; KTMShane699: run clickers fully in and out to exaggerate.
Enzo asks weight in street clothes; Touratech asks weight with clothing and helmet; others just say 'weight'.
Keefer 2025 describes stinkbug as rear high; Keefer 2021 lists it under sag 'too high'. Wording 'sag too high/low' is ambiguous between the number and the rear ride height.
Keefer fork article links headshake to fast rebound; MXA/Bones links on-throttle headshake to slow rebound or stiff fork; Teknik says reduce rebound.
Keefer 2020/2021: stiffer compression. Keefer 2024: more oil, heavier spring or more damping.
Forum posters split between soft fork, too much rebound, weight distribution, brake bite; fork height direction depends on bike.

gaps: No source gave a number of rides/hours before judging a revalve, or a standard tuner re-valve policy beyond Race Tech's stated guarantee.
No MX tuner source defined 'buck', 'pogo', 'spiky', 'chopper', 'dead', 'settle', 'wheel tracking' or 'front-end feel' explicitly.
Only one full MX tuner intake form obtained (Enzo); Pro Circuit model-specific form PDFs not opened.
First-hit vs series distinction is covered by packing articles but no source framed it as an explicit question to ask.
Bylines on MXA 'Bare Bones' pages conflict with page metadata (Bones Bacon vs Jody Weisel/Tom Hinz).
